title: COP31 opens: Bangladesh asks for grants, not loans, and three times more adaptation money
excerpt: The climate summit runs in Antalya from 9 to 20 November. Bangladesh will cite a $15.2 billion yearly climate toll but has set no compensation figure.
content:
The UN climate summit, COP31, opens on Monday, 9 November, in Antalya, Turkey, and runs until 20 November. Bangladesh is going with one central message: money for adaptation and for loss and damage should come as grants, not loans, bdnews24.com reported.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will attend the high-level segment from 10 to 12 November, according to Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo.

What Bangladesh is asking for

  • A threefold increase in adaptation finance. The delegation has not said from what baseline or by when.
  • Grant-based climate finance, so that adaptation and loss and damage funding “must not compound our sovereign debt burden,” in Mintoo’s words.
  • A larger Loss and Damage Fund that actually pays out on the ground, with simpler access, including through the Green Climate Fund.
  • Dedicated indicators and resources for the Global Goal on Adaptation, and keeping the 1.5°C limit in the mitigation talks.
  • Technology transfer for farming and water security, and help designing bankable projects.

Bangladesh will present a figure of US$15.2 billion a year in climate-related economic losses, which Mintoo linked to a World Bank assessment. But it will not name a compensation sum. “Negotiations do not work around a single pre-set compensation sum,” he said. Bangladesh will negotiate alongside the Least Developed Countries group, the G77 and the Climate Vulnerable Forum.

Why loans are the sore point

A Climate Debt Risk Index published in November 2025 by the Dhaka think tank Change Initiative put Bangladesh in its “high risk” group. It found Bangladesh received about $2.70 in climate loans for every $1 in grants, took $3.4 billion in climate-related loans between 2009 and 2022, and received only $1.41 billion for adaptation between 2002 and 2023, a small fraction of the roughly $230 billion its National Adaptation Plan says is needed by 2050.

Who said what

“The procedural barriers confronting vulnerable nations and affected populations must be dismantled,” said Shama Obaed Islam, state minister for foreign affairs. Saimum Parvez, special assistant to the prime minister, said Bangladesh’s main goal is “securing concrete, trackable progress on implementation support.” Climate expert Professor Ainun Nishat was blunter: “Political declarations and procedural milestones are routinely secured, but delivery lags.”

Why it matters

Most climate adaptation work in Bangladesh’s coastal, char and haor areas is delivered by NGOs, often with donor money that is shrinking. Whether COP31 produces more grant-based adaptation and loss and damage funding, and whether it can be reached by national and local organisations directly, will shape what climate programmes look like over the next five years.

What to watch

The prime minister’s statement on 10 to 12 November, any new pledges to the Loss and Damage Fund and the Adaptation Fund, and the final text on the Global Goal on Adaptation on 20 November.
